blocks.text: At Daniel 2:4b, the book shifts from Hebrew to Aramaic and remains in Aramaic until 8:1. This language pattern crosses a common division between Daniel’s court tales and visions, so it is important literary evidence; yet it does not by itself establish when each section was written or prove a particular theory of the book’s composition. The statue’s metals portray a succession of kingdoms, ultimately displaced by the enduring kingdom symbolized by the stone. Daniel names Nebuchadnezzar as the head of gold but does not name every later kingdom. Readers should therefore begin with the chapter’s literary and Hellenistic horizons, while recognizing that Jewish and Christian identifications of the kingdoms are competing interpretations rather than conclusions explicitly supplied by the chapter.
